claims.text: The as-prepared MnNiSi-based material has a large magnetocaloric effect but insufficient mechanical robustness under cyclic operating conditions.
Controlled annealing can promote targeted grain-boundary segregation in MnNiSi-based magnetocaloric material.
Controlled annealing can induce nanometer-scale precipitates in MnNiSi-based magnetocaloric material.
Thermomechanical processing can refine or otherwise tune alloy microstructure.
Grain refinement can enhance mechanical strength while retaining satisfactory ductility.
Precipitate formation can improve alloy strength.
The proposed nanoscale precipitates strengthen the material by arresting dislocation motion.
Grain-boundary enrichment contributes beneficially to mechanical strengthening.
Appropriate metallic-material post-treatment can reduce premature fatigue failure and improve fatigue performance.
The proposed controlled annealing will improve the tensile strength of MnNiSi-based material relative to an untreated control.
The proposed controlled annealing will improve the fatigue resistance of MnNiSi-based material relative to an untreated control.
The annealed material will retain a magnetocaloric effect comparable to that of the untreated baseline.
The engineered grain size, grain boundaries, and precipitates can be produced without interfering with the magnetostructural transition.
Maintaining the integrity of the magnetostructural transformation preserves the magnetocaloric effect.
The hypothesis is intended to hold during near-room-temperature operation under cyclic magnetic fields typical of magnetic refrigeration.
Annealing parameters that cause unwanted phase transformations may degrade magnetocaloric performance.
Annealing temperature and duration must be optimized to balance mechanical improvement against magnetocaloric retention.
Annealing may cause subtle shifts in the magnetostructural transition temperature.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant mechanical improvement, or degradation of magnetic entropy change or transition temperature, would falsify the hypothesis.
